title: Toilets through a Canadian winter
summary: Keep a household's toilet working when the ground is frozen: dig the pit before freeze-up, run a bucket toilet with urine kept apart, store frozen waste safely, and bury it before the spring melt carries it into wells and streams. The main dangers are waste reaching drinking water in the thaw, skipped hand-washing, and anyone climbing into a pit or tank.

steps.text: Before snow falls, pick the toilet site: at least 30 m (100 ft) from every well, spring, lake and stream (UAF Extension for wells, King County for surface water), on ground that slopes away from the well, and away from where meltwater runs. Ontario's legal minimum is 15 m from a drilled well, lake or stream and 30 m from a dug well (TBDHU). See [Latrines and distances](#ref/reference_sanitation/latrines_and_distances).
Mark the well head, the toilet site and any buried water line with tall stakes, so snow can't hide them.
Dig the pit in autumn, before frost sets in. Frozen ground stops a spade, and on the Prairies frost goes 1.5 to 3.5 m deep (PFRA).
steps.warn: Keep a second person at the top while anyone is in the hole, and support or slope loose sides. Pits collapse, even in soil that was firm when dug: line the top 0.5 to 1 m, and in loose soil build a raised pit instead (WEDC Guide 24).

steps.text: Build the slab or bench at least 150 mm (6 in) above the ground, leaving room under it for a frozen pile to grow (WEDC Guide 29). Hang the door to open inward so drifts can't block it (TBDHU).
Make a winter seat from 5 cm (2 in) rigid foam board, with the hole cut to match the seat (UAF Extension).

If it is a ventilated improved pit (VIP) latrine, WEDC says to seal the vent pipe when the cold weather comes, because it pulls cold air through the pit (WEDC Guide 29). Ontario's code asks for a screened vent duct on a privy (TBDHU), so check local rules. With the vent sealed, pit gas leaves through the seat: keep the lid shut between uses and flames away.

Indoors, set up a bucket toilet: a 19 L (5 gal) pail lined with two heavy garbage bags, cat litter, ash or sawdust in the bottom, and a lid kept shut (King County). Catch urine separately in a jug or funnel (see [the compost toilet](#guides/build_compost_toilet)).

Tie off the bags each day. Store them in a lidded bin in a protected place such as a garage (King County), away from food, animals, the well and any ground where meltwater runs, until you can bury them.
steps.warn: Breakdown stops below zero and starts again in the warm (WEDC Guide 29). Don't count on freezing to make waste safe: handle it like fresh sewage.

steps.text: Empty urine onto soil away from wells, paths and water, on ground that doesn't drain towards them (Compendium: urine can go into soil or a soak pit, ideally more than 30 m from drinking water). Frozen ground won't take it in, so pour it where meltwater won't carry it to a well or stream. Rinse the jug with water only.
steps.warn: Never put bleach in a urine jug or bucket. Stored urine gives off ammonia (Compendium), and bleach with ammonia makes a toxic gas.

steps.text: Put a hand-washing station by every toilet: an insulated jug of water that you top up with warm water, soap, and a towel or paper to dry hands (WEDC Guide 29).
Wash with soap and water after every visit, then dry your hands completely before going back out into the cold (CDC hand FAQ).

Bury the stored bags as soon as the ground will take a spade, before the melt runs. Use a pit at least 30 m (100 ft) from wells and water, with its bottom well above the high water table (TBDHU asks for at least 0.9 m), and cover the bags with at least 0.5 m of soil, the cover WEDC gives for a full latrine pit (King County, WEDC Guide 23). If you can, dig this pit in autumn and keep it covered, so you aren't waiting on the thaw. Wear waterproof gloves, boots and goggles (CDC workers).
steps.warn: Wash hands with soap at once afterwards, and keep children away while you work.

steps.text: In spring, check the pit and slab before anyone stands at the edge. Ground that was firm when frozen goes soft as it thaws (WEDC Guide 29).
steps.warn: Never climb into a pit, vault or septic tank, even to rescue someone (see [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space)). The air in them can kill in seconds, and would-be rescuers die too.

notes:
## Why winter is different

- **Frozen ground holds water like a floor.** Liquid from a pit is unlikely to soak away until it thaws (WEDC Guide 29).
- **Breakdown stops below zero.** Microbes in a pit go quiet and only start again in the warm months, so the pit fills faster in winter (WEDC Guide 29). Don't count on freezing to make waste safe; handle frozen waste as untreated.
- **Below about −10 °C, droppings freeze before they slump.** They build a frozen tower under the seat. Leave a big gap between the slab and the pit contents, or use a long slot instead of a round hole, so people can shift position as the pile grows (WEDC Guide 29).
- **People skip a long, cold walk.** Put the latrine close to the house, where it is sheltered from wind (WEDC Guide 29).
- **Vent pipes work against you.** A ventilated pit latrine draws cold air through the pit all winter, so WEDC says to seal its vent when the cold sets in (WEDC Guide 29). Ontario's code asks for a screened vent duct on a privy (TBDHU), so check local rules, and with the vent sealed keep the seat lid shut. See [the VIP latrine guide](#guides/build_vip_latrine).

## Frost and digging

- On the Canadian Prairies natural ground freezes to 1.5 to 3.5 m. In Saskatchewan, water pipes are generally buried below 2.4 m, and as deep as 4.0 m where the snow cover may be removed, such as road crossings (PFRA).
- Snow cover protects buried pipe from freezing (PFRA). A trampled path can drive the frost down and freeze a line under it, so don't run the toilet path over a buried water line (UAF Extension).
- In very cold places building stops in the coldest months, and aid agencies have used diggers on snow vehicles to dig latrine pits (WEDC Guide 29). With hand tools, **dig in autumn**: one pit for the whole winter, with a lid.
- Concrete that isn't cured properly for cold conditions can be weak and liable to collapse (WEDC Guide 29). Pour slabs before frost, or build the floor from heavy timber.
- If you must dig into frozen ground that will thaw, lay two poles, pipes or planks under the slab, reaching at least 1 m past the hole on each side, so the load spreads onto firm ground (WEDC Guide 29).

## Choosing a winter toilet

| Option | Good for | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| Bucket toilet indoors, bags stored frozen | Any cold; nights, the sick, children and the old | Bags need a safe store until you can bury them (King County), and burying before the melt |
| Pit privy dug in autumn, near the house | A household for the whole winter | Frozen pile, cold seat, thaw collapse (WEDC Guide 29) |
| Urine kept apart from faeces | Cutting what you store: about 500 L of urine a person a year against 50 L of faeces (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 6) | A urine jug outdoors freezes |
| Cathole dug away from water | Backcountry only, and frozen ground often stops it | Snowmelt can wash waste into water, so keep 60 m (200 ft) from water (Alberta Health Services) |

In the backcountry, Alberta Health Services says the best winter choice is to pack waste out; otherwise dig catholes about 15 cm (6 in) deep, at least 60 m (200 ft) from water, camps and trails (Alberta Health Services).

## Bucket toilets in the cold

- The set-up and daily routine are in [Bucket toilet](#ref/reference_sanitation/bucket_toilet). A house toilet bowl lined with two bags works the same way (King County). If the house is going cold, drain and protect the toilet first: see [winterising the house](#guides/skill_winterise_house), and [sewer backup](#guides/safety_sewer_backup) if the drains are blocked.
- **Keep urine out of the bag.** Urine is most of the volume. It normally leaves the body free of germs but can pick them up from faeces (EcoSanRes Fact Sheet 6). Bags then stay smaller and drier. The [compost toilet guide](#guides/build_compost_toilet) shows a simple funnel diverter.
- **Store bags frozen.** King County says to keep tied bags in a protected place such as a garage. Use a lidded bin in an unheated garage, shed or outbuilding, away from people, food and animals. Keep it well away from the well and from ground where meltwater runs, so a split bag or tipped bin at the thaw can't reach water.
- **Clean without mixing chemicals.** Wipe the seat with bleach solution from [Bleach solutions](#ref/reference_sanitation/bleach_solutions), but keep bleach out of anything that has held urine. See [the chemicals card](#ref/reference_chemicals/never_mix).

## The outhouse in winter

- **Seat:** 5 cm (2 in) rigid foam board cut to the seat's shape feels warm even in the cold (UAF Extension). Fit a tight lid over the hole between uses (WEDC Guide 29).
- **Door:** opening inward, so you can get in without shovelling (TBDHU).
- **Roof:** sloped to shed snow (UAF Extension).
- **Slab:** at least 150 mm above the ground, with a lid over the hole when it's not in use (WEDC Guide 29).
- **Pile:** raise the slab or bench to give the frozen tower room; it slumps when it warms (WEDC Guide 29).
- **Spring:** what works in winter may not work during breakup and spring drainage (UAF Extension). Check for water in the pit and soft ground at the edges.
- **Heat and light:** Keep fuel heaters, stoves, lanterns and candles out of a small closed outhouse. Health Canada says not to run kerosene, propane or oil heaters and lamps in enclosed spaces unless they are made for indoor use, and not to run fuel-burning equipment in a shed (Health Canada CO). Pit gas also includes methane (WEDC Guide 25; OMAFRA gases), which can burn or explode in a closed space, so use a battery torch. See [Carbon monoxide](#browse/hazards/co_gas) and [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space).

## Water and wells

- Ontario's code for pit privies, which also covers composting and bucket toilets, sets them at least 15 m from a drilled well, 30 m from a dug well and 15 m from a lake or stream, with the pit bottom at least 0.9 m above the high water table or bedrock (TBDHU). Humanitarian guides use 30 m from any water source and 1.5 m above the water table: see [Latrines and distances](#ref/reference_sanitation/latrines_and_distances). Use the larger figures where you can.
- Snow hides streams, ditches and well heads. Stake them in autumn.
- Waste left on or in snow gets washed into water sources when the snow melts, so keep it away from places where meltwater drains (Alberta Health Services). Frozen ground is largely impermeable (WEDC Guide 29), so early meltwater is likely to run over the surface instead of soaking in.
- If waste has reached a well, treat the water as unsafe until you have tested or disinfected it: see [testing water](#guides/test_water) and [shock chlorinating a well](#guides/skill_shock_chlorinate_well).

## Before the thaw

1. Pick up any waste on the snow near the house, the path and the well.
2. Bury stored bags as soon as you can dig: at least 30 m from wells and water, with the pit bottom well above the high water table (TBDHU asks for at least 0.9 m), under at least 0.5 m of soil. That is the cover WEDC gives for a full latrine pit, deep enough to walk over and to keep animals and flies out (WEDC Guide 23).
3. Wear waterproof gloves, rubber boots and goggles. Don't touch your face, and wash your hands with soap straight after. Clean contaminated work clothes daily in a 0.05 % chlorine solution, which CDC gives as 1 part household bleach to 100 parts water (CDC workers). That matches about 5 % bleach: check your label, use plain unscented bleach, and never mix it with other cleaners.
4. Check the outhouse slab and pit edges as the ground softens (WEDC Guide 29).

Never climb into a pit, vault or septic tank. Latrine pits give off ammonia, methane and carbon dioxide (WEDC Guide 25). Methane is combustible, so keep flames and sparks away from a pit (OMAFRA gases), and the air in a closed pit can kill: see [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space).

## Hand-washing in the cold

- Warm and cold water remove the same germs, so cold water is fine. Dry your hands completely: germs spread more easily from wet hands (CDC hand FAQ).
- When the water is very cold, people, especially children, stop washing. Insulate the water container, pour in hot water now and then, and give people something to dry their hands on, because wet hands feel colder as they dry (WEDC Guide 29).
- With no water at all, use an alcohol sanitiser of more than 60 % alcohol; it doesn't work on greasy or dirty hands (Alberta Health Services). How to wash: [Handwashing](#ref/reference_sanitation/handwashing). A [tippy tap](#guides/build_tippy_tap) by the door saves water.
- Wet hands and clothes speed up frostbite and hypothermia: see [Cold](#browse/hazards/cold).
